title: The Winding Number and the Global Cauchy Theorem

items.title: Tagged sums approximate a contour integral within oscillation times length
items.strategy: Subdivide the parameter interval at the partition points; the restrictions of $\gamma$ reassemble to $\gamma$ under an increasing reparametrisation, so the integral is the sum of the subarc integrals. On each subarc replace the integrand by its value at the tag: the difference is the integral of $f-f(\gamma(\xi_i))$, bounded by the oscillation on that subarc times the subarc length by the ML estimate, and the constant integrates to the endpoint increment. Sum and use additivity of arc length. State the bound with the oscillation, not with a limit, so later uses get a modulus of continuity.

items.title: A continuous function holomorphic off a single point is holomorphic
items.strategy: Two steps. Goursat with one exceptional point gives $\int_{\partial T}f=0$ for every filled triangle contained in the open set, the exceptional point being allowed inside, outside or on the boundary. Morera's triangle criterion then upgrades continuity plus vanishing triangle integrals to holomorphy on the whole open set, the exceptional point included.

items.title: A contour integral of a jointly continuous, parameter-holomorphic integrand is holomorphic
items.strategy: Let $\varphi$ be continuous on $\gamma^\ast\times\Omega$ with $\varphi(w,\cdot)$ holomorphic for each $w$. Fix a closed disc $K\subseteq\Omega$. The product $\gamma^\ast\times K$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^4$, hence compact, so $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous there; $\gamma$ is uniformly continuous on its parameter interval. Take the uniform partitions $P_n$ of mesh $(b-a)/n$ with left-endpoint tags: the tagged sums are finite linear combinations of the holomorphic functions $z\mapsto\varphi(\gamma(\xi),z)$, and the previous lemma bounds their distance to $F$ by the common oscillation times $L(\gamma)$, uniformly on $K$. So $F$ is a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions; Weierstrass convergence finishes.

items.title: A holomorphic logarithm is a primitive of the logarithmic derivative
items.strategy: If $L$ and $h$ are holomorphic on an open $U$ with $\exp\circ L=h$, then $h$ is nowhere zero because $|\exp v|=\exp(\operatorname{Re}v)>0$. Differentiate $\exp(L)=h$ by the chain rule and the derivative of $\exp$: $L'\exp(L)=h'$, so $L'=h'/h$. Apply it to $h(z)=z-p$ on a disc missing $p$ to get $L'(z)=1/(z-p)$.

items.title: A disc missing $p$ carries a holomorphic logarithm of $z-p$
items.strategy: On $D(c,r)$ with $p\notin D(c,r)$ the function $h(z)=z-p$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, so the published disc lemma supplies a holomorphic $L$ with $\exp\circ L=h$; the preceding corollary gives $L'(z)=1/(z-p)$. Record that any two such $L$ differ by a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$, since their difference is continuous with values in $\ker\exp$ on a connected set.

items.title: A contour missing a point subdivides into arcs lying in discs that miss it
items.strategy: The trace is a continuous image of a compact interval, hence compact, hence closed and bounded; so $d=\inf\{|w-p|:w\in\gamma^\ast\}$ is positive, for otherwise $p$ would lie in the closed set $\gamma^\ast$. Uniform continuity of $\gamma$ gives $\delta>0$ with $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|<d$ whenever $|t-s|<\delta$; take any partition of mesh below $\delta$. Then $\gamma([t_i,t_{i+1}])\subseteq D(\gamma(t_i),d)$ and $p\notin D(\gamma(t_i),d)$ because $|p-\gamma(t_i)|\ge d$. Cover the degenerate case of a constant parameter interval.

items.title: Continuous logarithms and continuous arguments along a contour
items.strategy: Definition only. A continuous logarithm of $\gamma-p$ along $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ with $p\notin\gamma^\ast$ is a continuous $\lambda:[a,b]\to\mathbb C$ with $\exp(\lambda(t))=\gamma(t)-p$ for every $t$; a continuous argument is $\theta=\operatorname{Im}\lambda$. Distinguish this from a holomorphic logarithm branch on an OPEN set, which is a holomorphic $L$ with $\exp\circ L=\mathrm{id}-p$ there: the first lives on the parameter interval and always exists, the second lives on the plane and need not. Fix the branch ambiguity of each: an additive constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

items.title: Every contour missing a point admits a continuous logarithm, unique up to a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$
items.strategy: Existence: subdivide as in the subdivision lemma, take a holomorphic branch $L_i$ of $\log(z-p)$ on the $i$th disc, and define $\lambda$ on $[t_i,t_{i+1}]$ as the accumulated increment $\lambda(t_{i})+L_i(\gamma(t))-L_i(\gamma(t_i))$, starting from any $\lambda(a)$ with $\exp\lambda(a)=\gamma(a)-p$, which exists by surjectivity of $\exp$ onto the punctured plane. Induct on $i$: the two formulas agree at each $t_i$ by construction, so $\lambda$ is continuous, and $\exp\lambda(t)=\gamma(t)-p$ throughout. Uniqueness: two continuous logarithms differ by a continuous function with values in $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$ on the connected interval, hence by a constant.

items.title: The integral of $dz/(z-p)$ along a contour is the increment of a continuous logarithm
items.strategy: With the subdivision and the branches $L_i$ of the previous two results, the fundamental theorem for contour integrals evaluates $\int_{\gamma|[t_i,t_{i+1}]}dz/(z-p)=L_i(\gamma(t_{i+1}))-L_i(\gamma(t_i))$, since $L_i'(z)=1/(z-p)$ is continuous on the disc. Sum over $i$ using additivity of the contour integral over the subdivision; the sum telescopes to $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)$ by the definition of $\lambda$. The value is independent of the chosen $\lambda$ because two choices differ by a constant.

items.title: The winding number of a closed contour about a point off its trace
items.strategy: Definition only. For a closed rectifiable contour $\gamma$ and $p\notin\gamma^\ast$, set $n(\gamma,p)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\gamma dz/(z-p)$. The integral exists because $z\mapsto 1/(z-p)$ is continuous on the compact trace and $\gamma$ is rectifiable. Say explicitly that the definition is about the parametrised contour and not about its trace.

items.title: The winding number of a closed contour is an integer
items.strategy: By the logarithm-increment theorem $2\pi i\,n(\gamma,p)=\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)$ for a continuous logarithm $\lambda$ of $\gamma-p$. Since $\gamma$ is closed, $\exp\lambda(b)=\gamma(b)-p=\gamma(a)-p=\exp\lambda(a)$, so $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)\in\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$. Hence $n(\gamma,p)\in\mathbb Z$. No differentiability of $\gamma$ is used anywhere, which is what makes the proof valid for the rectifiable contours this library defines.

items.title: The winding number is the increment of a continuous argument divided by $2\pi$
items.strategy: Write $\lambda=\log|\gamma-p|+i\theta$ with $\theta=\operatorname{Im}\lambda$ a continuous argument. Taking moduli in $\exp\lambda=\gamma-p$ gives $\operatorname{Re}\lambda(t)=\log|\gamma(t)-p|$, which returns to its initial value on a closed contour, so $\lambda(b)-\lambda(a)=i(\theta(b)-\theta(a))$ and $n(\gamma,p)=(\theta(b)-\theta(a))/2\pi$. This is the sense in which the index counts turns.

items.title: The winding number is constant on each connected component of the complement of the trace
items.strategy: Show $p\mapsto n(\gamma,p)$ is continuous on $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$. With $d=\operatorname{dist}(p_0,\gamma^\ast)>0$ and $|p-p_0|<d/2$, the identity $1/(z-p)-1/(z-p_0)=(p-p_0)/((z-p)(z-p_0))$ and the ML estimate give $|n(\gamma,p)-n(\gamma,p_0)|\le L(\gamma)|p-p_0|/(\pi d^2)$. A continuous integer-valued function on a connected set is constant, so the index is constant on each component; components of an open subset of the plane are open, so the function is locally constant.

items.title: The exterior of a closed disc in the plane is path-connected
items.strategy: Given $|z-c|>R$ and $|w-c|>R$, put $\rho=\max(|z-c|,|w-c|)$. Move $z$ radially to $c+\rho(z-c)/|z-c|$: the modulus stays between $|z-c|$ and $\rho$, hence above $R$. Do the same for $w$. Join the two resulting points along the circle of radius $\rho$ about $c$, which is path-connected as the image of the unit circle under $x\mapsto c+\rho x$, the unit circle being path-connected in dimension two. Concatenate the three paths.

items.title: The complement of a compact plane set has exactly one unbounded connected component
items.strategy: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb C$ be compact, hence bounded, say $K\subseteq\overline D(0,R)$. The exterior $E=\{|z|>R\}$ is connected by the previous lemma and lies in $\mathbb C\setminus K$, so it lies inside a single component $U_\infty$, which is therefore unbounded. Any other component is disjoint from $U_\infty$, hence from $E$, hence contained in $\overline D(0,R)$ and bounded. Handle $K=\varnothing$ separately: then the complement is the connected plane, and the statement still holds with one component.

items.title: The winding number vanishes on the unbounded component of the complement of the trace
items.strategy: The trace is compact, so by the previous theorem $\mathbb C\setminus\gamma^\ast$ has exactly one unbounded component $U_\infty$. For $p$ there with $\operatorname{dist}(p,\gamma^\ast)$ large, the ML estimate gives $|n(\gamma,p)|\le L(\gamma)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(p,\gamma^\ast))<1$; being an integer it is $0$. Points of arbitrarily large distance exist in $U_\infty$ because it is unbounded and $\gamma^\ast$ is bounded. Constancy on the component transfers the value $0$ to all of $U_\infty$.

items.title: Reversal negates and concatenation adds winding numbers
items.strategy: Both identities are the corresponding contour-integral identities applied to $1/(z-p)$: reversal negates the integral and concatenation of composable closed contours adds it. State the hypotheses that keep the results closed contours, namely that the concatenated pieces are composable and the result closed.

items.title: A circle traversed $k$ times has winding number $k$ inside and $0$ outside
items.strategy: For $k\ge1$, $\gamma_k(t)=a+r\exp(ikt)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ is an increasing reparametrisation of the $k$-fold concatenation of the positively oriented circle, so its integral of $1/(z-a)$ is $k$ times the circle's, which is $2\pi i$; hence $n(\gamma_k,a)=k$. For $k=0$ the contour is constant and the integral is $0$; for $k<0$ use reversal. The open disc $D(a,r)$ is connected and misses the trace, so local constancy gives $n(\gamma_k,z)=k$ throughout it. The set $|z-a|>r$ is contained in the unbounded component, so the index is $0$ there.

items.title: Complex chains, their traces, and cycles
items.strategy: Definition only. A complex chain in an open $\Omega$ is a finite list $\Gamma=((m_0,\gamma_0),\dots,(m_{r-1},\gamma_{r-1}))$ of integers $m_k$ and rectifiable contours $\gamma_k$ with trace in $\Omega$, written $\sum_{k<r}m_k\gamma_k$; its trace is the union of the traces of those $\gamma_k$ with $m_k\ne0$. Its boundary is the function on $\mathbb C$ sending $q$ to $\sum\{m_k:\gamma_k \text{ ends at } q\}-\sum\{m_k:\gamma_k\text{ starts at }q\}$, and $\Gamma$ is a CYCLE when that function is identically zero. Define sum and negation of chains by list concatenation and by negating every coefficient. Note that the empty list is a cycle and that a list of closed contours is a cycle, so the definition includes the single closed contour as the case $r=1$, $m_0=1$. Deliberately no free abelian group is invoked: chains are lists, equality of chains is equality of lists, and no theorem below claims that two differently presented chains are equal.

items.title: Integration over a complex chain and the index of a chain
items.strategy: Definition only. For a chain $\Gamma=\sum_{k<r}m_k\gamma_k$ and $f$ continuous on its trace, set $\int_\Gamma f\,dz=\sum_{k<r}m_k\int_{\gamma_k}f\,dz$, and for $p$ off the trace set $n(\Gamma,p)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)$. Both are finite sums of existing integrals. Record that for $r=1$, $m_0=1$ and $\gamma_0$ closed this is the winding number already defined, so the notation is consistent.

items.title: Chain integration and the index are additive in the chain, and reverse with it
items.strategy: Additivity in the chain is the definition together with finite-sum laws: appending lists adds the defining sums, and negating every coefficient negates them. Combine with the reversal and concatenation laws for a single contour to get the sign and sum rules in the form used later: $n(-\Gamma,p)=-n(\Gamma,p)$, $n(\Gamma_1+\Gamma_2,p)=n(\Gamma_1,p)+n(\Gamma_2,p)$, and the same identities for $\int_\Gamma f\,dz$. Include the empty chain, whose integral and index are $0$.

items.title: The index of a cycle about a point off its trace is an integer
items.strategy: For each $k$ choose a continuous logarithm $\lambda_k$ of $\gamma_k-p$ along $\gamma_k$; the logarithm-increment theorem gives $\int_{\gamma_k}dz/(z-p)=\lambda_k(b_k)-\lambda_k(a_k)$. Hence $\exp\bigl(\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)\bigr)=\prod_k\bigl((\gamma_k(b_k)-p)/(\gamma_k(a_k)-p)\bigr)^{m_k}$ by the addition formula for $\exp$ and the integer-power laws in the multiplicative group of nonzero complex numbers. Group the factors by the point of $\mathbb C$ at which they are evaluated: the exponent of $(q-p)$ is exactly the value of the boundary function at $q$, which vanishes because $\Gamma$ is a cycle. So the exponential is $1$ and the integral lies in $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$. Contours with $m_k=0$ contribute nothing; the empty cycle gives $0$.

items.title: The integral of a continuous derivative over a cycle is zero
items.strategy: If $F$ is a primitive of a continuous $f$ on an open set containing the trace of a cycle $\Gamma$, the fundamental theorem evaluates each $\int_{\gamma_k}f\,dz$ as $F(\gamma_k(b_k))-F(\gamma_k(a_k))$. Summing with the coefficients $m_k$ and grouping by evaluation point, the coefficient of $F(q)$ is the boundary function of $\Gamma$ at $q$, which is zero. This is where boundary-zero, rather than the weaker requirement that every piece be closed, does its work.

items.title: The index of a cycle is locally constant off its trace and vanishes far from it
items.strategy: Apply the corresponding single-contour results termwise: each $p\mapsto n(\gamma_k,p)$ is continuous off $\gamma_k^\ast$, so the finite combination is continuous off the trace of $\Gamma$, and it is integer-valued by the previous theorem, hence locally constant. The ML bound gives $|n(\Gamma,p)|\le\sum_k|m_k|L(\gamma_k)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(p,\Gamma^\ast))$, so the index is $0$ once the distance exceeds that finite bound. Conclude that $\{p\notin\Gamma^\ast: n(\Gamma,p)=0\}$ is open and contains the complement of some closed disc.

items.title: Null-homologous cycles and homologous cycles in an open set
items.strategy: Definition only. A cycle $\Gamma$ with trace in an open $\Omega$ is null-homologous in $\Omega$ when $n(\Gamma,p)=0$ for every $p\in\mathbb C\setminus\Omega$; two cycles in $\Omega$ are homologous in $\Omega$ when their difference is null-homologous, equivalently when their indices agree at every point outside $\Omega$. Say explicitly that the notion depends on $\Omega$ and not on $\Gamma$ alone, and that null-homologous does not mean equal to the empty chain.

items.title: Homologically simply connected complex domains
items.strategy: Definition only. A complex domain $\Omega$ is homologically simply connected when every cycle with trace in $\Omega$ is null-homologous in $\Omega$. Keep the qualifier "homologically" in the name and in every use: this page develops no other notion of simple connectivity, and none from its declared prerequisites is invoked.

items.title: Star-shaped plane domains are homologically simply connected
items.strategy: Let $\Omega$ be star-shaped and open, $\Gamma$ a cycle in $\Omega$ and $p\notin\Omega$. Then $z\mapsto 1/(z-p)$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$, so it has a primitive there by the star-shaped primitive theorem, and its derivative is continuous. The cycle integral of a continuous derivative vanishes, so $n(\Gamma,p)=0$. Every convex open set, in particular every disc and the whole plane, is star-shaped.

items.title: On a convex open set the difference quotient is an average of the derivative along the segment
items.strategy: For $z,w$ in a convex open $V$ on which $f$ is holomorphic, the segment from $z$ to $w$ lies in $V$ and $f'$ is continuous there because a holomorphic function is smooth. The fundamental theorem for contour integrals along that segment gives $f(w)-f(z)=\int_{[z,w]}f'(\zeta)\,d\zeta$, and the parametric form of the integral rewrites this as $(w-z)\int_0^1 f'(z+t(w-z))\,dt$. The identity holds for $w=z$ as well, both sides being $0$; and dividing by $w-z$ when $w\ne z$ exhibits the difference quotient as the displayed average.

items.title: The filled difference quotient of a holomorphic function is jointly continuous
items.strategy: Let $g(w,z)$ be $(f(w)-f(z))/(w-z)$ off the diagonal and $f'(z)$ on it. Off the diagonal joint continuity is the algebra of continuous functions. At a diagonal point $(a,a)$ take a disc $D(a,\rho)$ with closure in $\Omega$; for $w,z\in D(a,\rho)$ the segment formula gives $g(w,z)=\int_0^1 f'(z+t(w-z))\,dt$, valid on and off the diagonal, so $|g(w,z)-g(a,a)|\le\sup_{|\zeta-a|<\rho}|f'(\zeta)-f'(a)|$. Uniform continuity of $f'$ on a compact disc makes that supremum small, giving continuity at $(a,a)$.

items.title: The filled difference quotient is holomorphic in each variable separately
items.strategy: The filled quotient is symmetric in its two arguments, so it is enough to treat one of them. With $z$ fixed, the published exceptional-extension lemma says $\zeta\mapsto g(\zeta,z)$ is continuous on $\Omega$ and holomorphic on $\Omega\setminus\{z\}$. The removability lemma of this page upgrades that to holomorphy on all of $\Omega$, the filled point included.

items.title: The Cauchy transform of a cycle is holomorphic off its trace, with the expected derivatives
items.strategy: Apply the published differentiation lemma for Cauchy integrals to each contour of the chain on the open set $V=\mathbb C\setminus\Gamma^\ast$: each $z\mapsto(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{\gamma_k}\varphi(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-n}\,d\zeta$ is holomorphic on $V$ with derivative $n$ times the next one. A finite integer combination of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, and the derivative relation passes through the combination.

items.title: Dixon's glued function is entire and vanishes at infinity
items.strategy: Let $\Gamma$ be a cycle null-homologous in the open $\Omega$ and $f$ holomorphic on $\Omega$. Put $h_0(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma g(\zeta,z)\,d\zeta$ for $z\in\Omega$, which is holomorphic by the parameter theorem of this page applied to the jointly continuous, separately holomorphic filled quotient. Put $\Omega_0=\{z\notin\Gamma^\ast:n(\Gamma,z)=0\}$, open by local constancy, and $h_1(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}d\zeta$, holomorphic there. On $\Omega\cap\Omega_0$ linearity splits the integral and the index term is zero, so $h_0=h_1$; null-homology gives $\Omega\cup\Omega_0=\mathbb C$, so the two glue to an entire $h$. Finally $|h(z)|\le ML(\Gamma)/(2\pi\operatorname{dist}(z,\Gamma^\ast))$ on the far part of $\Omega_0$, so $h$ is bounded and $h(z)\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$.

items.title: Cauchy's integral formula for a null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: The glued function $h$ is entire and bounded, so Liouville makes it constant, and the constant is $0$ because $h(z)\to0$ at infinity. For $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ the first expression for $h$ splits by linearity into $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}d\zeta - n(\Gamma,z)f(z)$, so that difference is zero, which is the formula. State it for every $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ and note that no connectedness of $\Omega$ is required.

items.title: Cauchy's theorem for a null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: Fix $z\in\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$. Such a $z$ EXISTS, and the reason is not that the trace has empty interior: that is a stronger claim about rectifiable curves which this library has not established and which must not be asserted. The trace of a chain is a finite union of continuous images of compact parameter intervals, hence compact, hence closed and bounded; and $\Gamma^\ast\subseteq\Omega$, so $\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast=\varnothing$ would force $\Omega=\Gamma^\ast$, making the nonempty open $\Omega$ a bounded clopen subset of $\mathbb C$. Bounded gives $\Omega\ne\mathbb C$, and $\mathbb C$ is connected under the published plane dictionary, so its only clopen subsets are $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb C$ — a contradiction. Then apply the integral formula to $F(\zeta)=(\zeta-z)f(\zeta)$, which is holomorphic on $\Omega$ and vanishes at $z$: the left side is $n(\Gamma,z)F(z)=0$ and the right side simplifies to $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f$, since $(\zeta-z)$ cancels on the trace, where $\zeta\ne z$. Treat the empty cycle and the empty $\Omega$ separately; both give $0$.

items.title: Holomorphic integrals agree on homologous cycles
items.strategy: If $\Gamma_0$ and $\Gamma_1$ are homologous in $\Omega$ then $\Gamma_0-\Gamma_1$ is a null-homologous cycle in $\Omega$, so Cauchy's theorem gives $\int_{\Gamma_0-\Gamma_1}f=0$; the chain laws split that into $\int_{\Gamma_0}f-\int_{\Gamma_1}f$.

items.title: The higher-derivative form of the global Cauchy formula
items.strategy: On the open set $\Omega\setminus\Gamma^\ast$ the function $z\mapsto n(\Gamma,z)f(z)$ agrees with the Cauchy transform $F_1$ of $f$ over $\Gamma$. The index is locally constant, so on a neighbourhood of any such $z$ it is a constant $k$, and differentiating the identity $kf=F_1$ there $n$ times, using $F_m'=mF_{m+1}$ from the transform lemma and induction, gives $n(\Gamma,z)f^{(n)}(z)=(n!/2\pi i)\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-n-1}\,d\zeta$. Include $n=0$ as the formula already proved.

items.title: Every holomorphic function on a homologically simply connected domain has a primitive
items.strategy: Every closed rectifiable contour in $\Omega$ is a cycle, hence null-homologous, so Cauchy's theorem gives $\int_\gamma f=0$ for all of them. The published path-independence criterion, which is stated for a complex domain and a continuous $f$, converts that into the existence of a primitive. Holomorphic functions are continuous, so the criterion applies.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a homologically simply connected domain has a holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: The logarithmic derivative $f'/f$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ because $f$ is nowhere zero and holomorphic functions are smooth. Take a primitive $F$ by the previous theorem, adjusted by a constant so that $\exp(F(z_0))=f(z_0)$ at one point, which is possible since $\exp$ is onto the punctured plane. Then $f\exp(-F)$ has zero derivative on the domain, hence is constant, and the constant is $1$; so $\exp\circ F=f$. Uniqueness: two holomorphic logarithms differ by a continuous function into $\ker\exp=2\pi i\mathbb Z$ on a connected set, hence by a constant in $2\pi i\mathbb Z$.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on such a domain has holomorphic roots of every positive order
items.strategy: With $\exp\circ L=f$ from the previous theorem, set $q=\exp(L/m)$ for a positive integer $m$. Then $q$ is holomorphic and $q^m=\exp(L)=f$ by the addition formula and induction on $m$. Note that $q$ is nowhere zero, and that the choice of $L$ shifts $q$ by an $m$th root of unity.

items.title: Equivalent characterisations of a homologically simply connected domain
items.strategy: Prove the cycle $(i)\Rightarrow(ii)\Rightarrow(iii)\Rightarrow(iv)\Rightarrow(vi)\Rightarrow(i)$ and $(ii)\Rightarrow(v)\Rightarrow(vi)$ for a complex domain $U$: (i) every cycle in $U$ is null-homologous; (ii) every holomorphic function on $U$ has a primitive; (iii) every nowhere-zero holomorphic function on $U$ has a holomorphic logarithm; (iv) $1/(z-p)$ has a primitive on $U$ for every $p\notin U$; (v) every holomorphic integral over every cycle in $U$ vanishes; (vi) $\int_\Gamma dz/(z-p)=0$ for every cycle $\Gamma$ in $U$ and every $p\notin U$. Three of the arrows are already proved on this page. For (iii) to (iv), differentiate $\exp(g(z))=z-p$ to get $(z-p)g'(z)=1$. For (iv) to (vi) and (ii) to (v), the cycle integral of a continuous derivative vanishes. (vi) to (i) is the definition of the index restated, and it is where the equivalence closes.

items.title: The principal logarithm is the normalised holomorphic branch on the slit plane
items.strategy: The slit plane $\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ is open, connected and star-shaped with respect to $1$, hence homologically simply connected, so the identity function on it has a holomorphic logarithm $F$; normalise $F(1)=0$. Then $\operatorname{Re}F(z)=\log|z|$ from $|\exp v|=\exp(\operatorname{Re}v)$. To identify $\operatorname{Im}F(z)$ with the principal argument, run $t\mapsto\operatorname{Im}F(1+t(z-1))$ along the segment, which starts at $0$; if it ever reached $\pm\pi$ the corresponding point would equal $-|w|$, a negative real, which the slit plane excludes, so by the intermediate value theorem the imaginary part stays in $(-\pi,\pi)$. Uniqueness of the principal argument then gives $F=\operatorname{Log}$, and $F'=1/z$ makes $\operatorname{Log}$ holomorphic there with derivative $1/z$.

items.title: Conventions for chains, cycles and the homological adjective on this page
items.strategy: Prose only. Record four conventions and why each is taken: a chain is a finite list, so no free abelian group is imported and no theorem here claims two differently presented chains are equal; a cycle is a chain whose boundary function vanishes, which is what makes the integral of a continuous derivative over it vanish, and it is weaker than requiring each piece to be closed; the adjective is 'homologically simply connected' throughout, because the notion defined here is about indices and this page invokes no other notion of simple connectivity; and the winding number is attached to the parametrised contour, not to its trace, with the false statement on the companion page as the witness. Justify, do not survey.

title: The Winding Number and the Global Cauchy Theorem — Examples

items.title: The unit circle traversed three times has index $3$ at every interior point
items.strategy: Take $\gamma(t)=\exp(3it)$ on $[0,2\pi]$ and apply the circle theorem with $a=0$, $r=1$, $k=3$: the index is $3$ on $|z|<1$ and $0$ on $|z|>1$. Then exhibit the continuous logarithm $\lambda(t)=3it$, verifying $\exp(\lambda(t))=\gamma(t)$ directly rather than by appeal to the existence theorem; its imaginary part is a continuous argument running from $0$ to $6\pi$, and $6\pi/(2\pi)=3$ recovers the same index.

items.title: A figure-eight cycle has indices $+1$ and $-1$ in its two loops
items.strategy: Present the figure eight as the chain $\gamma_1+\gamma_2$ where $\gamma_1$ is the positively oriented circle about $-1$ of radius $1/2$ and $\gamma_2$ the negatively oriented circle about $1$ of the same radius. By chain additivity the index at a point is the sum of the two circle indices, so it is $+1$ near $-1$, $-1$ near $1$, and $0$ outside both discs. Note that the two loops share no point, so the trace is the disjoint union of the two circles.

items.title: The boundary cycle of a round annulus has index $1$ inside the annulus and $0$ on either side
items.strategy: For $0<r_1<r_2$ let $\Gamma$ be the positively oriented circle about $p$ of radius $r_2$ minus the positively oriented circle of radius $r_1$. Chain additivity and the circle theorem give the index $1-1=0$ for $|z-p|<r_1$, $1-0=1$ for $r_1<|z-p|<r_2$, and $0-0=0$ for $|z-p|>r_2$. Draw only the conclusion the computation licenses: $\Gamma$ is null-homologous in the open annulus $r_1<|z-p|<r_2$, because every point of the complement of that annulus has index $0$. Name the open set before naming the homology, since the notion depends on it.

items.title: The winding numbers of a keyhole contour about the origin and about an excluded point
items.strategy: Build the keyhole as a cycle: the large positively oriented circle of radius $R$ about $0$, plus the small negatively oriented circle of radius $\varepsilon$ about $0$, joined by two opposite radial segments that cancel in the boundary count. Compute the index by additivity, at points OFF the trace: $0$ inside the small disc, $1$ in the annulus and off the radial segments, $0$ outside. The two segments have the same trace and both carry coefficient $1$, so that radius belongs to $\Gamma^\ast$ and no index is defined on it. Show the two segments contribute nothing to the index because they cancel as a chain, and check the boundary function is zero so the chain really is a cycle.

items.title: A continuous argument computed along a spiralling contour
items.strategy: Take $\gamma(t)=(1+t)\exp(2\pi i t)$ on $[0,1]$ and $p=0$. The function $\lambda(t)=\log(1+t)+2\pi i t$ is continuous with $\exp\lambda(t)=\gamma(t)$, so it is a continuous logarithm; its imaginary part is a continuous argument increasing by $2\pi$. The contour is not closed, so no winding number is defined, yet the logarithm increment $\log 2+2\pi i$ is exactly $\int_\gamma dz/z$. This separates the logarithm-increment theorem from the integrality theorem.

items.title: Dixon's gluing traced on the boundary cycle of an annulus
items.strategy: Take $\Omega=\{1/2<|z|<3\}$ and let $\Gamma$ be the positively oriented circle of radius $2$ minus the positively oriented circle of radius $1$, both centred at $0$; the preceding example makes $\Gamma$ null-homologous in $\Omega$. For $f(z)=1/z$ on $\Omega$, identify $\Omega_0$ explicitly, write out $h_0$ and $h_1$, check they agree on the overlap, and confirm $n(\Gamma,z)f(z)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma f(\zeta)(\zeta-z)^{-1}\,d\zeta$ at an explicit $z$ with $1<|z|<2$ by computing both sides from the circle integrals of integer monomials.

items.title: Every cycle in a round annulus has one period, that of the central circle
items.strategy: Let $A=\{r_1<|z|<r_2\}$ and $C$ the positively oriented circle of an intermediate radius. For a cycle $\Gamma$ in $A$ put $k=n(\Gamma,0)$; then $\Gamma$ and $kC$ have the same index at every point of $\mathbb C\setminus A$, since the complement has the two pieces $|z|\le r_1$ and $|z|\ge r_2$ and the index is constant on the components meeting them. So the two cycles are homologous in $A$ and $\int_\Gamma f=k\int_C f$ for every holomorphic $f$ on $A$. Illustrate with $f(z)=1/z$, whose period is $2\pi i$.

items.title: The winding number is the circulation of the planar vortex field
items.strategy: Prose. For a piecewise-$C^1$ closed contour $\gamma$ missing the origin, the parametric form of the contour integral splits $\int_\gamma dz/z$ into the two real line integrals of the vector fields $(x,y)\mapsto(x,y)/(x^2+y^2)$ and $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)/(x^2+y^2)$. The second is the published closed-but-not-exact field on the punctured plane, and its circulation is $2\pi n(\gamma,0)$; the first is the gradient of $\tfrac12\log(x^2+y^2)$ and contributes nothing around a closed contour. So the failure of closed to imply exact on the punctured plane and the nonvanishing of the winding number are one fact seen twice. Say which convention is used for the identification.

items.title: A connected plane domain that is not homologically simply connected
items.strategy: Refute: every complex domain is homologically simply connected. Witness: the annulus $A=\{1/2<|z|<2\}$, which is open and connected, together with the positively oriented unit circle $C$ in it. The point $0$ lies outside $A$ and $n(C,0)=1\ne0$, so $C$ is not null-homologous in $A$. Verify connectedness of $A$ and that $C$ has trace in $A$.

items.title: A nonvanishing holomorphic function on a domain with no holomorphic logarithm
items.strategy: Refute: every nonvanishing holomorphic function on a complex domain has a holomorphic logarithm. Witness: the identity function on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$. A holomorphic logarithm would in particular be a continuous $L$ with $\exp L(z)=z$ on the punctured plane, which the published theorem forbids; the published statement is about continuity alone and so is stronger than what is needed here. Alternatively, integrating $L'=1/z$ around the unit circle would give $0$ while the integral is $2\pi i$. Give both refutations and say which hypothesis of the positive theorem fails.

items.title: The winding number depends only on the trace of the closed contour
items.strategy: The claim is false. The unit circle traversed once and traversed twice have the same trace $\{|z|=1\}$ and indices $1$ and $2$ at the origin. Refute by computing both from the circle theorem. Point out that the same phenomenon already appeared for contour integrals, and that the index is defined from the parametrised contour precisely because of this.

items.title: Every cycle in a connected plane domain is null-homologous in that domain
items.strategy: The claim is false, and it is the claim that would make the homological hypothesis in the global Cauchy theorem vacuous. Refute with the unit circle in the annulus $\{1/2<|z|<2\}$, whose index at $0$ is $1$ while $0$ lies outside the annulus. Add the consequence that the conclusion of Cauchy's theorem also fails there, since $\int_C dz/z=2\pi i\ne0$ with $1/z$ holomorphic on the annulus.

title: Holomorphic Functions of Several Complex Variables

items.title: Complex $m$-space and its real coordinate dictionary
items.strategy: Prose. Fix $m\ge1$ and let $\mathbb C^m$ be the set of functions $m\to\mathbb C$, so coordinates are $z_k$ for $k<m$, matching the library's indexing of $\mathbb R^n$ from $0$. Writing $z_k=x_k+iy_k$ identifies $\mathbb C^m$ with $\mathbb R^{2m}$ by $z\mapsto(x_0,y_0,\dots,x_{m-1},y_{m-1})$; record that this is the chosen ordering and that the alternative grouping is a different bijection. Check the Euclidean norm $\lVert z\rVert=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|z_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$ agrees with the $\mathbb R^{2m}$ Euclidean norm under it, so open sets, convergence, compactness and completeness transfer verbatim, and note the $m=1$ case reduces to the published plane dictionary. Also record the $\mathbb C$-vector-space structure and that a subset is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded.

items.title: Balls, polydiscs and the distinguished boundary in $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. For $a\in\mathbb C^m$ and a polyradius $r$ with $r_k>0$ for $k<m$, define the open polydisc $\Delta_r(a)=\{z:|z_k-a_k|<r_k\text{ for all }k<m\}$, its closure, and its distinguished boundary $\Gamma_r(a)=\{z:|z_k-a_k|=r_k\text{ for all }k<m\}$, presented as the product of the $m$ circles. Define the ball by the Euclidean norm. Say explicitly that for $m\ge2$ the distinguished boundary is a proper subset of the topological boundary, and that a scalar $r$ abbreviates the constant polyradius. Note that a polydisc is convex, hence star-shaped, and that each of its one-variable slices is a disc.

items.title: Holomorphic functions on an open subset of $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. $f:U\to\mathbb C$ with $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ open is complex differentiable at $a$ when there is a $\mathbb C$-linear $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ with $f(a+h)=f(a)+L(h)+r(h)$ and $\lVert h\rVert^{-1}|r(h)|\to0$; $L$ is then unique and written $Df(a)$. Holomorphic on $U$ means complex differentiable at every point. State that $\mathbb C$-linear means additive and homogeneous over $\mathbb C$, not merely over $\mathbb R$, and that at $m=1$ this is the published notion because a $\mathbb C$-linear functional on $\mathbb C$ is multiplication by a scalar. Do NOT put continuity or local boundedness into the definition: the point of this page is that they are consequences or, in the separate case, theorems.

items.title: Separately holomorphic functions
items.strategy: Definition only. $f:U\to\mathbb C$ is separately holomorphic when, for every $a\in U$ and every $k<m$, the slice $\zeta\mapsto f(a_0,\dots,a_{k-1},\zeta,a_{k+1},\dots,a_{m-1})$ is holomorphic in the published one-variable sense on the open set of $\zeta$ for which the point lies in $U$. Record that no continuity in the remaining variables is asked, and that the slice domains are open because $U$ is.

items.title: Wirtinger operators in $\mathbb{C}^m$
items.strategy: Definition only. At a point where the $2m$ real partial derivatives of $f$ exist, set $\partial_{z_k}f=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_k}f-i\partial_{y_k}f)$ and $\partial_{\bar z_k}f=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_k}f+i\partial_{y_k}f)$ for $k<m$, the partial derivatives being those of the published real definition under the coordinate dictionary. Record the differential identity $Df(h)=\sum_{k<m}(\partial_{z_k}f)h_k+\sum_{k<m}(\partial_{\bar z_k}f)\overline{h_k}$ at a point of real total differentiability, and that at $m=1$ these are the published Wirtinger derivatives.

items.title: A real-linear functional on $\mathbb{C}^m$ is complex linear exactly when its antiholomorphic part vanishes
items.strategy: Every $\mathbb R$-linear $T:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C$ is uniquely $T(h)=\sum_{k<m}c_kh_k+\sum_{k<m}d_k\overline{h_k}$: get $c_k,d_k$ from the values of $T$ at $e_k$ and $ie_k$ by solving the two-by-two system, and check uniqueness by evaluating at those same vectors. Then $T$ is $\mathbb C$-linear iff $T(ih)=iT(h)$ for all $h$, and substituting the representation gives $-2i\sum_kd_k\overline{h_k}=0$ for all $h$, hence every $d_k=0$; conversely a sum of $c_kh_k$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. Include $m=1$ and the zero functional.

items.title: A holomorphic function of several variables is continuous and separately holomorphic
items.strategy: Continuity at $a$: the defining expansion gives $|f(a+h)-f(a)|\le|L(h)|+|r(h)|$, and $|L(h)|\le C\lVert h\rVert$ since a linear functional on $\mathbb C^m$ is bounded on the unit sphere by the standard-basis expansion. Separate holomorphy: restrict the expansion to $h=\xi e_k$, so $f(a+\xi e_k)-f(a)=L(e_k)\xi+r(\xi e_k)$ with $|r|/|\xi|\to0$; hence the slice is complex differentiable at $a_k$ with derivative $L(e_k)$, and that derivative equals $\partial_{z_k}f(a)$.

items.title: Multi-indexed power series in $\mathbb{C}^m$ and their absolute convergence
items.strategy: Definition only. Reuse the published multi-index conventions for $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb N^m$ indexed from $0$, and add the complex monomial $z^\alpha=\prod_{k<m}z_k^{\alpha_k}$. Say that $\sum_{\alpha}c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely at $z$ when for one, equivalently every, bijection $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^m$ the resulting complex series converges absolutely; the set $\mathbb N^m$ is countable, and absolute convergence and the sum are independent of the bijection by the published complex rearrangement theorem, so the sum is well defined and written $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$. Define uniform absolute convergence on a set by a summable majorant, so the Weierstrass test applies. Do not introduce a second notion of unordered sum.

items.title: The Cauchy kernel expands as an absolutely and uniformly convergent multi-indexed geometric series
items.strategy: Fix $a$, a polyradius $r$ and $z$ with $|z_k-a_k|\le\theta r_k$ for a single $\theta<1$. For $\zeta$ on the distinguished boundary $\Gamma_r(a)$, each factor $1/(\zeta_k-z_k)$ is $\sum_{j}(z_k-a_k)^j/(\zeta_k-a_k)^{j+1}$ by the one-variable geometric series, converging absolutely since the ratio has modulus at most $\theta$. Multiplying the $m$ series and using the Cauchy-product/rearrangement theorem gives $\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-z_k)^{-1}=\sum_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$, with the majorant $\prod_k\theta^{\alpha_k}/r_k$ summing to $\prod_k(r_k(1-\theta))^{-1}$. Conclude absolute convergence uniform in $\zeta\in\Gamma_r(a)$ and in $z$ on the closed subpolydisc.

items.title: The iterated Cauchy integral formula on a polydisc
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on the open polydisc $\Delta_\rho(a)$ and separately holomorphic there, and let $r_k<\rho_k$ for $k<m$. Induct on $m$. At each step apply the published one-variable circle formula in the variable $\zeta_k$, whose slice is holomorphic on the disc of radius $\rho_k$; the remaining variables are held fixed, so no interchange of integrals is performed anywhere and Fubini is not invoked. Joint continuity is what makes each successive integrand continuous on the circle, so each contour integral exists and the next application is legitimate. The result is the iterated integral over the $m$ circles of $f(\zeta)\prod_{k<m}(\zeta_k-z_k)^{-1}$, divided by $(2\pi i)^m$, valid for every $z\in\Delta_r(a)$. State it as an iterated integral, not as an integral over the distinguished boundary.

items.title: A continuous separately holomorphic function is the sum of an absolutely convergent power series with Cauchy-integral coefficients on every smaller polydisc
items.strategy: Substitute the kernel expansion into the iterated Cauchy formula. The expansion converges uniformly in $\zeta$ on each circle of integration and absolutely, so the sum may be taken through each of the $m$ contour integrals in turn by the published uniform-limit interchange, applied to the partial sums of a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb N^m$; uniformity of the remaining integrand in the outer variables is what licenses the next interchange, and the majorant of the kernel lemma supplies it. The result is $f(z)=\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ with $c_\alpha$ the iterated integral of $f(\zeta)\prod_k(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$ over $(2\pi i)^m$, converging absolutely and uniformly on every closed subpolydisc. The identification $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ is NOT available here — it needs termwise differentiation, which is the next theorem — so neither the title nor the Statement of this item may claim it; it is recorded in cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth.

items.title: An absolutely convergent multi-indexed power series is holomorphic and differentiates termwise
items.strategy: Suppose $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ converges absolutely at some point of every polyradius direction, so that on a closed subpolydisc $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|\theta^{|\alpha|}\prod r_k^{\alpha_k}<\infty$. Show the sum $g$ is complex differentiable at each interior point with $\mathbb C$-linear differential $h\mapsto\sum_{k<m}\bigl(\sum_\alpha\alpha_kc_\alpha(z-a)^{\alpha-e_k}\bigr)h_k$: expand $((z-a)+h)^\alpha$ by the multinomial expansion, isolate the constant and first-order terms, and bound the remainder by the majorant series with a factor $\lVert h\rVert^2$, using that $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha||\alpha|^2\theta^{|\alpha|}\prod r_k^{\alpha_k}$ converges. Conclude that each derived series has the same convergence polydisc and that the coefficients are $\partial^\alpha g(a)/\alpha!$ by induction.

items.title: Osgood's lemma: continuous and separately holomorphic implies holomorphic
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ and separately holomorphic. Around each $a\in U$ choose a polydisc with closure in $U$; the expansion theorem writes $f$ as an absolutely convergent power series on a smaller polydisc, and the previous theorem makes that sum holomorphic there. Holomorphy is a local property, so $f$ is holomorphic on $U$. Together with the earlier proposition this makes the three conditions equivalent for continuous functions: complex differentiability, local power-series representability, and separate holomorphy.

items.title: Holomorphic functions of several variables are smooth and their complex derivatives are holomorphic
items.strategy: By Osgood's lemma and the expansion theorem a holomorphic $f$ is locally a convergent power series; termwise differentiation gives every $\partial_{z_k}f$ as a convergent power series on the same polydisc, hence holomorphic, and the real partial derivatives of every order exist and are continuous by the same expansion in the real coordinates. Iterate to obtain $C^\infty$ and $\partial^\alpha f$ holomorphic for every multi-index, together with $c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$.

items.title: The coefficients of a convergent multi-indexed power series are its derivative coefficients, hence unique
items.strategy: If $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha=\sum_\alpha c'_\alpha(z-a)^\alpha$ on a polydisc about $a$, both sums are holomorphic there and termwise differentiation gives $\alpha!c_\alpha=\partial^\alpha f(a)=\alpha!c'_\alpha$ for every $\alpha$; since $\alpha!\ne0$ the coefficients agree. Record the consequence that a function has at most one power-series representation about a given centre.

items.title: Cauchy estimates for mixed derivatives on a polydisc
items.strategy: From the coefficient formula, $c_\alpha$ is an iterated integral of $f(\zeta)\prod_k(\zeta_k-a_k)^{-\alpha_k-1}$ over $(2\pi i)^m$; bound each of the $m$ integrals by the ML estimate, with circle length $2\pi r_k$ and kernel modulus $r_k^{-\alpha_k-1}$. This gives $|c_\alpha|\le M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$ with $M$ the supremum of $|f|$ on the distinguished boundary, hence $|\partial^\alpha f(a)|\le\alpha!\,M\prod_{k<m}r_k^{-\alpha_k}$. Note the estimate uses only the distinguished boundary, not the whole topological boundary.

items.title: A bounded separately holomorphic function on a polydisc is Lipschitz on every smaller polydisc
items.strategy: Let $|f|\le M$ on $\Delta_\rho(a)$ with $f$ separately holomorphic, and let $\theta<1$. For $z,w$ in the closed polydisc of polyradius $\theta\rho$, telescope in one coordinate at a time: the difference $f(w)-f(z)$ is the sum over $k<m$ of the increments obtained by changing the $k$th coordinate from $z_k$ to $w_k$ with the earlier coordinates already changed. Each increment is a difference of one-variable holomorphic function values, bounded by $|w_k-z_k|$ times the supremum of the slice derivative on a segment in the disc of radius $\theta\rho_k$; that supremum is at most $M/((1-\theta)\rho_k)$ by the published Cauchy inequality, UNIFORMLY in the other coordinates because $M$ bounds $f$ everywhere. Summing gives a Lipschitz bound. This uses no continuity of $f$ in the remaining variables at any point.

items.title: Locally bounded and separately holomorphic implies holomorphic
items.strategy: Local boundedness gives, around each point, a polydisc on which $f$ is bounded; the Lipschitz lemma then makes $f$ continuous on a smaller polydisc, hence continuous on the whole open set since continuity is local. Osgood's lemma upgrades continuity plus separate holomorphy to holomorphy. State plainly that the local-boundedness hypothesis is what is removed by the Hartogs theorem, which is not available at this point in the reading order, and do not use that later theorem here.

items.title: For $C^1$ functions, holomorphy, complex linearity of the real derivative, and the Cauchy–Riemann system agree
items.strategy: For $f:U\to\mathbb C$ of class $C^1$ in the real coordinates, prove three equivalences. Holomorphy gives real total differentiability with the same differential, so the real derivative is $\mathbb C$-linear by uniqueness of the total derivative. Complex linearity of the real derivative is equivalent to the vanishing of every $\partial_{\bar z_k}f$ by the criterion lemma applied to the Wirtinger representation of the differential. Conversely, $C^1$ gives real total differentiability by the published continuous-partials theorem, and a $\mathbb C$-linear total derivative turns the real expansion into the complex one. Say explicitly that the $C^1$ hypothesis is used only in the last implication.

items.title: Sums, products and nonvanishing quotients of holomorphic functions are holomorphic
items.strategy: Work from the defining expansion. Additivity and scalar multiples are immediate. For a product, expand $f(a+h)g(a+h)$ using both expansions and collect: the first-order part is $f(a)Dg(a)+g(a)Df(a)$, a $\mathbb C$-linear functional, and the remainder is $o(\lVert h\rVert)$ using continuity of $f$ and the linear bound on $Dg(a)$. For a quotient with $g(a)\ne0$, use continuity of $g$ to keep it away from zero near $a$ and expand $1/g$ as in one variable. Record the resulting product and quotient rules for $\partial_{z_k}$.

items.title: Locally uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, with locally uniform convergence of all derivatives
items.strategy: A locally uniform limit $f$ of continuous $f_n$ is continuous. Each slice of $f$ is a locally uniform limit of the corresponding holomorphic slices, so it is holomorphic by the published one-variable Weierstrass convergence theorem; hence $f$ is continuous and separately holomorphic, and Osgood's lemma makes it holomorphic. For the derivatives, apply the Cauchy estimates on a polydisc to $f_n-f$: the bound is $\alpha!\sup_{\Gamma}|f_n-f|\prod_kr_k^{-\alpha_k}$, which tends to $0$ uniformly on the smaller polydisc.

items.title: The modulus of a holomorphic function on a closed polydisc is bounded by its supremum on the distinguished boundary
items.strategy: Let $f$ be continuous on the closed polydisc and holomorphic on its interior. Apply the one-variable boundary maximum-modulus principle in the first variable with the others fixed on their closed discs, then in the second, and so on; after $m$ steps every coordinate has been pushed to its circle. Each step is legitimate because the slice is continuous on the closed disc and holomorphic inside. Conclude $\sup_{\overline\Delta}|f|=\sup_{\Gamma}|f|$, and note this is stronger than the one-variable statement only in that the bounding set is far smaller than the topological boundary.

items.title: Holomorphic maps $\mathbb{C}^m \to \mathbb{C}^n$ and the complex Jacobian matrix
items.strategy: Definition only. $F:U\to\mathbb C^n$ with $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ open is holomorphic at $a$ when there is a $\mathbb C$-linear $L:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^n$ with $F(a+h)=F(a)+L(h)+r(h)$ and $\lVert r(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$; $L$ is unique. Define the complex Jacobian $J_{\mathbb C}F(a)$ as the matrix of $L$ in the standard bases, whose $(j,k)$ entry is $\partial_{z_k}F_j(a)$ for $j<n$, $k<m$, using the published matrix of a linear map over the field $\mathbb C$. Record that $n=1$ recovers the scalar definition.

items.title: A map into $\mathbb{C}^n$ is holomorphic exactly when each of its components is
items.strategy: If $F$ is holomorphic with differential $L$, then $F_j=\pi_j\circ F$ has differential $\pi_j\circ L$, which is $\mathbb C$-linear, and the remainder estimate passes to a component because $|r_j(h)|\le\lVert r(h)\rVert$. Conversely, if every $F_j$ is holomorphic with differential $L_j$, assemble $L(h)=(L_0(h),\dots,L_{n-1}(h))$, which is $\mathbb C$-linear, and bound $\lVert r(h)\rVert$ by the sum of the $|r_j(h)|$ using the norm comparison in $\mathbb C^n$; each term is $o(\lVert h\rVert)$ and there are finitely many. Cover $n=0$, where the statement is vacuous, and $n=1$.

items.title: The composite of holomorphic maps is holomorphic and its complex Jacobian is the product
items.strategy: Let $F:U\to V$ and $G:V\to\mathbb C^p$ be holomorphic at $a$ and $F(a)$. Substitute the expansion of $F$ into that of $G$: the first-order term is $DG(F(a))\circ DF(a)$, a composite of $\mathbb C$-linear maps, hence $\mathbb C$-linear. Bound the remainder by splitting it into $DG(F(a))$ applied to the remainder of $F$ and the remainder of $G$ evaluated at $DF(a)h+r_F(h)$, using the linear bound and continuity of $F$; both are $o(\lVert h\rVert)$. The Jacobian identity is the published matrix-of-a-composite theorem applied to the two differentials.

items.title: The complex Jacobian determinant of a composite of equidimensional holomorphic maps is the product
items.strategy: When $m=n=p$, the Jacobians are square matrices over $\mathbb C$, which is a commutative ring, so the published multiplicativity of the determinant applies to the chain-rule identity: $\det J_{\mathbb C}(G\circ F)(a)=\det J_{\mathbb C}G(F(a))\cdot\det J_{\mathbb C}F(a)$. Record the consequence that a biholomorphic map has nowhere-vanishing Jacobian determinant, obtained by applying this to a two-sided inverse.

items.title: A holomorphic function vanishing on a nonempty open subset of a domain vanishes identically
items.strategy: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ be a domain and $f$ holomorphic with $f=0$ on a nonempty open $W\subseteq U$. Put $A=\{z\in U:\partial^\alpha f(z)=0\text{ for every }\alpha\}$. It is closed in $U$ as an intersection of zero sets of continuous functions, nonempty since $W\subseteq A$, and open because at $a\in A$ the power-series expansion has all coefficients $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ equal to zero, so $f$ vanishes on a whole polydisc about $a$ and with it all its derivatives. Connectedness gives $A=U$, hence $f\equiv0$. State the theorem in the form the several-variable setting actually supports and say in the Statement itself that vanishing on a set with an accumulation point is NOT assumed and would not suffice.

items.title: The holomorphic functions on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^m$ have no zero divisors
items.strategy: The holomorphic functions on $U$ form a commutative ring under pointwise operations by the algebra proposition. If $fg\equiv0$ and $f\not\equiv0$, then $\{f\ne0\}$ is a nonempty open subset of $U$ on which $g$ vanishes, so $g\equiv0$ by the identity theorem. Record that connectedness of $U$ is essential and that the ring is nonzero because constants are holomorphic.

items.title: An interior local maximum of the modulus forces a scalar holomorphic function to be constant
items.strategy: Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $U\subseteq\mathbb C^m$ with $|f(z)|\le|f(a)|$ on a ball $B$ about $a$. For each $v$ with $\lVert v\rVert=1$ the slice $g_v(\xi)=f(a+\xi v)$ is holomorphic on a disc about $0$ by the chain rule, and $|g_v|$ has a local maximum at $0$, so $g_v$ is constant near $0$ by the published one-variable local maximum-modulus principle. Every point of a smaller ball has the form $a+\xi v$, so $f$ is constant on that ball; the identity theorem applied to $f-f(a)$ makes $f$ constant on $U$.

items.title: A bounded holomorphic function on all of $\mathbb{C}^m$ is constant
items.strategy: For fixed $z\in\mathbb C^m$ the slice $\xi\mapsto f(\xi z)$ is entire in one variable by the chain rule and bounded by the same bound, hence constant by the published Liouville theorem; evaluating at $\xi=0$ and $\xi=1$ gives $f(z)=f(0)$. Since $z$ was arbitrary, $f$ is constant. Note that no connectedness argument is needed and that $m=0$ is degenerate.

items.title: A nonconstant scalar holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^m$ is an open map
items.strategy: Let $f$ be holomorphic and nonconstant on a domain $U$, let $O\subseteq U$ be open and $a\in O$. Choose a polydisc $\Delta\subseteq O$ about $a$; the identity theorem forbids $f$ from being constant on $\Delta$, so there is $b\in\Delta$ with $f(b)\ne f(a)$. The set $W=\{\xi\in\mathbb C:a+\xi(b-a)\in\Delta\}$ is open and convex, hence a domain, and contains $0$ and $1$; $g(\xi)=f(a+\xi(b-a))$ is holomorphic on $W$ by the chain rule and nonconstant since $g(0)\ne g(1)$. The published one-variable open mapping theorem makes $g(W)$ open, and $f(a)=g(0)\in g(W)\subseteq f(\Delta)\subseteq f(O)$, so $f(a)$ is interior to $f(O)$. State that the theorem is about scalar targets and asserts nothing for maps into $\mathbb C^n$ with $n\ge2$.

items.title: Conventions on this page, and what the several-variable identity theorem does not say
items.strategy: Prose that justifies rather than surveys. Record: coordinates and multi-indices are indexed from $0$, matching the library's $\mathbb R^n$; holomorphic means complex differentiable, and local boundedness or continuity is never built into the definition, so Osgood's lemma and the locally bounded theorem are theorems rather than tautologies; the distinguished boundary, not the topological boundary, is what the Cauchy formula and the estimates use. Then state precisely why the identity theorem here is weaker than its one-variable ancestor: the hypothesis is a nonempty OPEN set of zeros, and an accumulation point of the zero set does not suffice, with the companion page's false statement carrying the witness. Do not describe what other pages contain.

title: Holomorphic Functions of Several Complex Variables — Examples

items.title: The power series of $z_0z_1$ on a bidisc centred away from the origin
items.strategy: Expand $f(z)=z_0z_1$ about $a=(1,1)$: writing $z_k=1+(z_k-1)$ gives $f(z)=1+(z_0-1)+(z_1-1)+(z_0-1)(z_1-1)$, a finite multi-indexed series with coefficients $c_{(0,0)}=c_{(1,0)}=c_{(0,1)}=c_{(1,1)}=1$ and all others $0$. Check the coefficients against $\partial^\alpha f(a)/\alpha!$ and note that a finite series converges absolutely everywhere.

items.title: The power series of $\exp(z_0+z_1)$ on every bidisc
items.strategy: Multiply the two one-variable exponential series and use the Cauchy-product theorem for absolutely convergent complex series to get $\exp(z_0+z_1)=\sum_{\alpha}z^\alpha/\alpha!$ over $\alpha\in\mathbb N^2$, absolutely convergent on every bidisc. Verify the coefficient identity $\partial^\alpha f(0)/\alpha!=1/\alpha!$ and confirm the majorant bound of the definition on a closed bidisc of polyradius $(R,R)$.

items.title: The power series of $z_0/(1-z_1)$ and the shape of its domain of convergence
items.strategy: On $\{|z_1|<1\}$ expand the geometric series to get $z_0/(1-z_1)=\sum_{j}z_0z_1^{\,j}$, that is $c_\alpha=1$ when $\alpha_0=1$ and $c_\alpha=0$ otherwise. Verify absolute convergence exactly when $|z_1|<1$, with no constraint on $z_0$, so the set of absolute convergence is an unbounded product region rather than a bounded polydisc. Note that this is a legitimate reading of the definition and that the function is holomorphic on the whole region by the termwise theorem.

items.title: The iterated Cauchy formula computed for $z_0z_1$ on a bidisc
items.strategy: Take $f(z)=z_0z_1$ on the unit bidisc and $r=(1/2,1/2)$. Compute the iterated integral $(2\pi i)^{-2}\oint\oint\zeta_0\zeta_1(\zeta_0-z_0)^{-1}(\zeta_1-z_1)^{-1}d\zeta_1\,d\zeta_0$ by evaluating the inner circle integral with the one-variable formula and then the outer one, and confirm the value is $z_0z_1$. Do the two integrals in the stated order and do not interchange them.

items.title: Cauchy estimates on a bidisc, computed and compared with the exact derivatives
items.strategy: For $f(z)=\exp(z_0+z_1)$, $a=0$ and polyradius $(r,r)$, the supremum of $|f|$ on the distinguished boundary is $\exp(2r)$, so the estimate gives $|\partial^\alpha f(0)|\le\alpha!\exp(2r)r^{-|\alpha|}$. The exact value is $1$; minimise the bound over $r$ to see how close the estimate comes for $\alpha=(1,1)$, and record that the bound is finite for every $r>0$ while the exact value does not depend on $r$.

items.title: Componentwise holomorphy checked for an explicit map $\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^3$
items.strategy: Take $F(z)=(z_0z_1, z_0+z_1, \exp(z_0))$. Verify each component is holomorphic directly from the definition or the algebra proposition, hence $F$ is holomorphic by the componentwise theorem, and write out the $3\times2$ complex Jacobian $\bigl(\partial_{z_k}F_j\bigr)$ explicitly at a general point and at $0$. Confirm the differential is $\mathbb C$-linear by exhibiting it as a matrix product.

items.title: The complex Jacobian and its determinant for $(z_0z_1, z_0+z_1)$
items.strategy: For $F(z)=(z_0z_1,z_0+z_1)$ compute $J_{\mathbb C}F(z)$ and $\det J_{\mathbb C}F(z)=z_1-z_0$. Identify the set where it vanishes, the diagonal, and check the multiplicativity corollary on the composite of $F$ with the linear swap $(w_0,w_1)\mapsto(w_1,w_0)$, whose Jacobian determinant is $-1$.

items.title: A function whose modulus attains its maximum only on the distinguished boundary of a bidisc
items.strategy: Take $f(z)=z_0z_1$ on the closed unit bidisc. Then $|f|\le1$ with equality exactly when $|z_0|=|z_1|=1$, that is exactly on the distinguished boundary. Exhibit a point of the topological boundary, say $(1,0)$, where $|f|=0$, so the topological boundary carries no information about the maximum. This is the concrete content of the distinguished-boundary corollary.

items.title: A nonzero holomorphic function on $\mathbb{C}^2$ whose zero set is an unbounded hyperplane
items.strategy: Refute: a holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb C^m$ that is not identically zero has isolated zeros. Witness: $f(z)=z_0$ on $\mathbb C^2$, holomorphic and not identically zero, with zero set $\{0\}\times\mathbb C$. Verify the zero set is unbounded and that no point of it is isolated in it, by exhibiting nearby zeros. Record that in one variable the corresponding claim is a published theorem, so the failure is a genuine several-variable phenomenon and not an oversight.

items.title: A holomorphic function on a domain in $\mathbb{C}^2$ vanishing on a set with an accumulation point vanishes identically
items.strategy: The claim is false, and it is exactly the one-variable identity theorem carried over without change. Refute with $f(z)=z_0$ on $\mathbb C^2$: its zero set is the hyperplane $z_0=0$, every point of which is an accumulation point of the zero set, and $f$ is not identically zero. Explain in the refutation which step of a one-variable proof breaks, namely that a zero of a nonzero holomorphic function of one variable has a finite order and an isolated zero, and that no such local factorisation is available here.

items.title: A bounded function of two real variables whose every coordinate slice is real analytic is continuous
items.strategy:
The claim is FALSE, and it is the real-variable analogue of thm-locally-bounded-separate-holomorphy — which is exactly why the several-variable holomorphic theorem is not a formality. Refute with the witness $f(x,y)=xy/(x^2+y^2)$ off the origin, $f(0,0)=0$, and prove ALL THREE of its properties here; this item is self-contained and cites no counterexample from another page. Bounded: $2|xy|\le x^2+y^2$ gives $|f|\le 1/2$ everywhere, and at the origin $f=0$. Every slice is real analytic on all of $\mathbb R$: for fixed $b
e0$ the slice $x\mapsto bx/(x^2+b^2)$ is a quotient of polynomials whose denominator never vanishes, and polynomials are real analytic as finite sums of products of constants and the identity, so the published closure theorem applies; for $b=0$ the slice is identically $0$, since $f(x,0)=0$ for $x
e0$ and $f(0,0)=0$. The same holds in the other variable by the symmetry $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$. Discontinuity at the origin is proved HERE in one line and not imported: along $y=x$ with $x
e0$ the value is $1/2$, which does not tend to $f(0,0)=0$, so $f$ is not continuous at the origin by def-metric-continuity. The published `cex-partial-derivatives-without-continuity` on `the-total-derivative-examples` states the discontinuity for the same function; name it in prose WITHOUT a wikilink and WITHOUT a deps edge — it lives on a B page, B pages are leaves, and validate-plan rejects the citation outright (error `b-leaf`). Say in the refutation which hypothesis of the holomorphic theorem has no real analogue: a one-variable bound on $f$ gives no bound on the slice derivative in the real case, whereas the Cauchy inequality supplies exactly that bound in the complex case, uniformly in the remaining coordinates.

items.title: Why local boundedness gives joint continuity here and nothing like it holds in the real case
items.strategy: Prose, justifying the hypotheses of the locally bounded theorem. State the real contrast concretely: the function that is $x_0x_1/(x_0^2+x_1^2)$ off the origin and $0$ at it is bounded and has a real-analytic slice in each coordinate through every point — the slice through the origin being identically zero — yet is not jointly continuous. Cite the false statement on this page, which carries the whole refutation including the discontinuity; do NOT cite the published `cex-partial-derivatives-without-continuity`, which is homed on the B page `the-total-derivative-examples` and is therefore not a legal deps target (validate-plan `b-leaf`). It may be named in prose without a wikilink. Then explain what makes the holomorphic case different: the one-variable Cauchy inequality converts a bound on the function into a bound on each slice derivative that is uniform in the remaining coordinates, and no real-variable hypothesis supplies such a bound.
